newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. Africa to test capital pact with business.
newsitem.headline: S. Africa to test capital pact with business.

text.p: Public Works Minister Jeff Radebe said the South African government agreed on Wednesday to test a plan to woo the private sector into infrastructure construction and ownership partnerships.
Radebe told Reuters in an interview that the cabinet had approved a broad framework for six pilot schemes including prisons, government housing and secure care facilities.
The contracts, known as Asset Procurement and Operating Partnerships (APOPs), would help South Africa address a 170 billion rand ($37.7 billion) infrastructure backlog.
The backlog is roughly equivalent to the entire 1996/97 budget, including interest and debt redemption.
"The project arose out of an instruction from Deputy President Thabo Mbeki at a conference earlier this year to strengthen the public and private sector partnership," Radebe said.
Mbeki met private sector investors from South Africa and abroad to discuss ways to help the government address the capital requirement for infrastructure.
"We had to look at innovative procurement techniques to allow government to avoid the up-front cost of infrastructure development.
"We're talking about things like correctional facilities, government housing and secure-care facilities for minors."
Radebe said the scheme was built around market-related returns for private sector operators who would finance and operate facilities, which the government would hire or lease.
"The programme offers good value for money for the government, it spreads the risk to the private sector and it gives us access to capital we do not have ourselves," he said.
In the arena of prisons alone, the programme could save the government "a couple of billion rand", he added.
Radebe said his department would release details of the scheme within days, detailing the framework and guidelines for the partnership proposal.
He said the pilot projects would be launched almost immediately and would be monitored by officials who would later draft a white paper on public works asset partnerships.
